Team Size, International Reach, and Citations in Management Research

Draft, 17 October 2026. Generated from paper_src.md by scripts/make_paper.py; all numbers and tables come from the result files.

Abstract

Do management papers written by larger teams, and by teams whose members are based in more than one country, receive more citations? We study 2,789 research articles published from 2008 to 2017 in Administrative Science Quarterly, Academy of Management Journal, Strategic Management Journal, and Organization Science, using OpenAlex bibliographic data and counting citations in the five calendar years after each article's publication year. On a complete-case sample of 2,768 articles, negative binomial models with journal-by-year fixed effects show that doubling the number of authors is associated with a citation rate 14% higher (rate ratio 1.139, 95% CI [1.081, 1.200]). This association survives controls for paper length, references, US authorship, multiple institutions, and authors' prior publications, and a range of robustness checks. Papers whose authors span more than one country have a citation rate about 7% higher than single-country papers of the same team size, but the estimate is borderline (rate ratio 1.066, 95% CI [0.993, 1.145], p = 0.077) and its significance depends on specification. A check that removes self-citations could be run only on a random subsample and is informative for team size but not for international reach. A planned extension on authors from countries outside the World Bank's high-income group was dropped because the historical income classification could not be obtained.

1. Introduction

Research is increasingly done in teams across nearly all fields, and teams typically produce more frequently cited research than individuals do (Wuchty, Jones, & Uzzi, 2007). In management research, too, most papers are team-authored: in our sample of articles in four leading management journals from 2008 to 2017, only 14.0% of articles with complete affiliation data are single-authored (Table 1).

If team papers are cited more, two different things may be going on. One is size: more authors bring more people who can present, circulate, and build on a paper, and more combined expertise. The other is reach: coauthors based in different countries may connect a paper to different scholarly communities and audiences. The two are hard to separate because they travel together. In our sample, 4.9% of solo papers have authors in more than one country (an author with affiliations in two countries), against 62.3% of four-author papers (Table 1). A finding that international papers are cited more could therefore simply reflect that they are written by larger teams. We test both, controlling team size flexibly when estimating the international effect.

On team size, the answer is yes, and robustly so. On international reach, it is a cautious maybe: the point estimate is positive and stable across specifications, but its confidence interval includes one in our main model. We report it as borderline rather than as support for the hypothesis.

2. Literature and hypotheses

Wuchty, Jones, and Uzzi (2007) use 19.9 million papers over five decades and 2.1 million patents. They report that research is increasingly done in teams across nearly all fields, that teams typically produce more frequently cited research than individuals do, and that this advantage has been increasing over time. Their results are detailed for the sciences and engineering, the social sciences, the arts and humanities, and patents.

Larivière, Gingras, Sugimoto, and Tsou (2015) analyze the relationship between collaboration and scientific impact in articles published between 1900 and 2011, using three indicators of collaboration: the number of authors, the number of addresses, and the number of countries in an article's byline. They report that an increase in the number of authors leads to an increase in impact from the beginning of the twentieth century onward, and that this is not due simply to self-citations. A similar trend is observed for the number of addresses and the number of countries. They also report that the constant inflation of collaboration since 1900 has resulted in diminishing citation returns: larger teams, and teams more diverse in institutional and country affiliation, are necessary to realize higher impact.

We test these relationships in four leading management journals, asking whether international reach matters beyond team size.

H1. Papers with more authors receive more citations.

H2. Papers whose authors are based in more than one country receive more citations than papers by teams of the same size based in one country.

3. Data and methods

3.1 Source and journals

Bibliographic data come from OpenAlex (openalex.org), which describes itself as "a free and open catalog of the world's research" and offers a public API; we collected the data on 17 October 2026. We identified the four journals through OpenAlex's source records by ISSN: Administrative Science Quarterly (0001-8392), Academy of Management Journal (0001-4273), Strategic Management Journal (0143-2095), and Organization Science (1047-7039; online 1526-5455). An earlier version of our notes listed 0170-8406 for Organization Science; in OpenAlex that ISSN belongs to Organization Studies, a different journal. We collected all works whose locations include one of the four journals, published 2008 to 2017, 3,656 records in all.

3.2 Sample

OpenAlex's document type "article" also includes front matter, book reviews, editorials, comments, and correction notices, and some records are duplicates or attributed to the wrong journal. We applied rules in a fixed order, each record taking the first that applied, and logged every dropped record and changed value with its reason. We dropped 383 records whose type is not article or review; 112 with no authors in OpenAlex or Crossref, all front matter or unsigned notices; 64 records from Soshiki Kagaku, a Japanese journal whose English title, Organizational Science, led to their attribution to Organization Science; 31 non-publisher copies of records already collected and 8 records with no publisher DOI and no journal version in OpenAlex; 11 duplicate records and attached correction notices; 246 non-research items, including 149 book reviews and 37 Academy of Management Journal editorials; 4 retracted articles; and 8 articles whose corrected publication year falls after 2017. Where OpenAlex had split one paper's citations across duplicate records, we merged them by citing-work identifier so that no citation is counted twice (20 papers). The result is 2,789 research articles: 209 in Administrative Science Quarterly, 755 in Academy of Management Journal, 1,028 in Strategic Management Journal, and 797 in Organization Science.

The publication year Y is the year a paper first appeared, usually online ahead of print. In a random check of 100 papers against Crossref, OpenAlex's publication year equaled the year the DOI was registered in 95, and the exact date matched in 80. Where OpenAlex's date was suspect (a record merged with a working-paper copy, a volume number inconsistent with the year, or a 1 January placeholder), we used the earliest Crossref date of registration, online, or print publication, which changed the publication year of 32 papers. Because both Academy of Management Journal and Strategic Management Journal moved to online-first publication during the period, some publication years contain more papers than others; journal-by-year fixed effects absorb these differences.

3.3 Citations

The outcome is the number of citations an article received in the five calendar years after its publication year, Y+1 to Y+5. The publication year itself is excluded because exposure within it ranges from days to almost a full year. Every article's window ends by 2022, so all windows are complete. OpenAlex records a per-year citation field (counts_by_year), but its documentation describes it as covering only the last ten years, and in our data it contains no year before 2012 for any article, so it omits the first years after publication for articles from 2008 to 2011. We therefore counted, for each article, the works that cite it by the citing work's publication year. Citation counts are highly skewed (mean 64.5, median 47; Table 1).

3.4 Authors and countries

Team size is the number of authors. Countries come from authors' affiliations. OpenAlex reports them as ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes, two letters (for example US, GB), according to its documentation for institutions and authorships. Where OpenAlex had no country for an author, we took it from the raw affiliation text only when that text names a country or a US state (65 authors); institution names alone were not interpreted. A paper is multi-country if its authors' affiliations span two or more countries. This includes a single author affiliated in two countries; a variant that counts only differences between authors is reported in Table 4. Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macao are kept as OpenAlex codes them, separately from mainland China; Section 4.5 shows what recoding them does.

For 21 of the 2,789 articles, at least one author's country remains unknown, so whether the paper is multi-country cannot always be determined. To estimate H1 and H2 on the same papers, we use the complete-case sample of 2,768 articles throughout.

3.5 Models

Citations are counts with strong overdispersion (negative binomial dispersion alpha = 0.51 in the H1 model), so we estimate negative binomial (NB2) models with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. All models include journal-by-year fixed effects, 40 cells, because citation levels and the timing of online-first publication differ by journal and year.

For H1, the main regressor is the natural logarithm of the number of authors, and we report the rate ratio for doubling team size. The logarithm allows each additional author to add less than the last. Among the team-size forms we compared (logarithm, linear count, categories, solo versus team), the logarithm fits best by BIC and the team-size categories by AIC; we report all four.

For H2, the regressor is the multi-country indicator, and team size is controlled with categories (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or more authors), so that "beyond team size" does not rest on a functional form for team size. A version with the logarithm of team size as the control is also reported.

To ask whether either measure is standing in for something else, we add candidate confounders one at a time and together: paper length (log pages), the number of references (log of one plus the count), whether any author is based in the United States, whether the authors span more than one institution, and the largest number of earlier papers any author had published in the sample. Some of these may be consequences of team size rather than causes, so they are checks, not part of the main model. Software: Python 3.14.7 with statsmodels 0.15.0, pandas 3.0.6, NumPy 2.5.4, SciPy 1.18.1, patsy 1.0.3, and matplotlib 3.11.2.

4. Results

4.1 Descriptive patterns

Table 1 describes the complete-case sample by team size. Mean citations in the five-year window rise from solo papers to four-author papers and are lower for papers with five or more authors. The share of multi-country papers rises steeply up to four authors and is similar for five or more.

4.2 Team size (H1)

Table 2 reports the main models. In column 1, doubling the number of authors is associated with a citation rate 14% higher (rate ratio 1.139, 95% CI [1.081, 1.200], p < 0.001). Column 2 shows the shape of the association: relative to solo papers, the rate ratio is 1.227 for two authors, 1.255 for three, 1.427 for four, and 1.235 for five or more, and every interval excludes one (Figure 1, panel A). The gain from adding authors rises up to four authors and does not continue beyond it; the five-or-more group is small and its interval is wide. H1 is supported.

4.3 International reach (H2)

Holding team size fixed with categories, papers whose authors span more than one country have a citation rate 7% higher than single-country papers (Table 2, column 3; rate ratio 1.066, 95% CI [0.993, 1.145], p = 0.077). With the logarithm of team size as the control, the estimate is 1.070 (p = 0.064; column 4). The estimate is positive but its confidence interval includes one. H2 is borderline: the data are consistent with a modest advantage for international teams, but they do not establish one at conventional levels of significance in our main specification.

4.4 Is either measure a proxy for something else?

Table 3 adds candidate confounders. The H1 estimate stays between 1.121 and 1.150 and remains significant in every row (largest p < 0.001). The H2 estimate changes little; it ranges from 1.061 to 1.083 and is 1.083 [1.006, 1.166] (p = 0.034) with all controls together. Neither measure appears to be standing in for these characteristics. The prior-publication measure counts only papers within our sample, from 2008 onward, and the multiple-institution measure is a lower bound, because authors without a matched institution are not counted.

4.5 Robustness

Table 4 and Figure 1, panel B, report the checks. For H1, the rate ratio for doubling team size stays between 1.125 and 1.141 (largest p < 0.001) across the full-sample checks; among teams only, it is 1.089 [1.003, 1.183]. Entered linearly, each additional author is associated with a 6.8% higher citation rate, and team papers have a rate ratio of 1.261 [1.147, 1.386] relative to solo papers.

For H2, the estimate stays between 1.064 and 1.072 in every full-sample check, with p-values between 0.041 and 0.093. It is significant at the 5% level with clustered standard errors (1.066, p = 0.049) and with capped citations (1.071, p = 0.041), and not in the other checks. The size of the H2 estimate is stable; its significance is not.

Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macao are coded separately from mainland China in OpenAlex, so a paper with authors in, say, Hong Kong and Taiwan counts as multi-country. Of the complete-case articles, 21 have an author based in Taiwan: 19 of them are multi-country, 2 have all authors in Taiwan, and 0 pair Taiwan only with mainland China; 126 articles have an author in Hong Kong or Macao. Recoding all three as China changes the multi-country status of 4 articles, 1 of them involving Taiwan, and moves the H2 estimate to 1.064 [0.991, 1.143]. Their coding does not affect the results.

4.6 Self-citations: a partial check

Larger teams have more authors who can cite the paper, so part of the team-size association could be mechanical. We counted citations excluding self-citations, defined as citing works that list any of the article's authors by OpenAlex identifier. Our data allowance permitted this for a seeded random subsample of 1,200 complete-case articles only; the remaining 1,568 could not be fetched, and nothing was substituted for them. This check is therefore partial.

In the subsample, the mean share of window citations that are self-citations rises with team size: 5.6% for solo papers, 6.6% for two authors, 7.4% for three, 7.8% for four, and 11.6% for five or more. For H1, removing self-citations moves the rate ratio for doubling team size from 1.131 [1.043, 1.227] to 1.112 [1.022, 1.209]: self-citation accounts for a small part of the team-size association, not most of it.

H2 cannot be assessed in the subsample. With all citations, before self-citations are removed, the subsample's H2 estimate is already 1.017 [0.915, 1.131], against 1.102 [1.005, 1.209] in the other 1,568 articles. The difference between the two halves is within what chance produces (difference in log rate ratios 0.080, SE 0.072, p = 0.26, treating the halves as independent), so the subsample appears noisy rather than different. But it cannot tell us whether self-citations matter for H2.

4.7 Differences across journals

Table 5 estimates the models separately by journal. The team-size association is significant in Strategic Management Journal and Organization Science and not in Administrative Science Quarterly or Academy of Management Journal. The multi-country estimate is positive in all four journals and significant in none. A pooled test does not reject equal slopes across journals for either hypothesis (H1 p = 0.196; H2 p = 0.599), so the pooled estimates are a reasonable summary, though the journal-level samples are small, especially for Administrative Science Quarterly.

5. Discussion

In four leading management journals, papers by more authors are cited more in the five years after publication, with the gain concentrated in the move from solo to small teams. The association holds across our proxy and robustness checks, and only a small part of it is attributable to self-citation in the subsample where we could measure it. This is consistent with the patterns reported by Wuchty et al. (2007) and Larivière et al. (2015), although our design differs from theirs and the estimates are not directly comparable.

The evidence on international reach is weaker. Papers spanning more than one country have a citation rate about 7% higher than single-country papers of the same team size, an estimate that is stable in size across every specification we tried, but whose confidence interval includes one in the main model and in most checks. We read this as borderline: the data do not rule out a modest advantage for international teams, and they do not establish one. One possible reason is that international collaboration is so closely tied to team size here that, once size is held fixed, little independent variation remains to estimate it precisely.

Limitations

Self-citations: partial check. Self-citations could be removed only for a random subsample of 1,200 of the 2,768 articles. The check informs H1 but not H2, and should be completed on the full sample.

Income-group extension dropped. We planned to ask whether it matters that a team includes an author based in a country outside the World Bank's high-income group. This requires each country's income group in each publication year from 2008 to 2017. The World Bank's data API, which we could reach, returned only the current classification in our tests: a request for Chile in 2010 returned Chile's current group, and so did the April 2010 edition in its archive of World Development Indicators. A historical classification would be needed [Unverified: we understand the World Bank publishes one as the file OGHIST.xlsx, "Historical classification by income," with its Country and Lending Groups data; the host serving it could not be reached, so we could not confirm the file or its contents]. We did not use the current classification as a substitute, because the groups in force in 2008 to 2017 may differ from it and we could not check by how much. The extension is therefore left out of this paper.

Observational design. The associations we estimate are not causal effects. Teams may form around more promising projects, and international teams may differ in topic or method in ways our controls do not capture.

Data coverage and measurement. All bibliographic data and citation counts come from OpenAlex as of 17 October 2026, and are only as complete as its records. Duplicate copies of a paper were matched by title and authors, so a copy under a different title can escape matching; we found one such case while checking the paper, a working-paper copy of a Strategic Management Journal article, and merged it by hand, and others may remain. Countries come from affiliations, which may not reflect where authors live or work. 21 articles with an author of unknown country are excluded from the analysis. Publication years were corrected only for records we had already collected, so a paper that OpenAlex dates to 2007 but that appeared in 2008 is not in the sample.

Scope. The sample covers four leading journals, and the results may not hold for management research published elsewhere.

Multiple checks. We report many robustness checks without correcting for multiple comparisons. They are meant to show how stable the estimates are rather than to provide separate tests, which is why we describe H2 as borderline rather than supported.

References

Larivière, V., Gingras, Y., Sugimoto, C. R., & Tsou, A. (2015). Team size matters: Collaboration and scientific impact since 1900. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(7), 1323–1332. https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.23266

Wuchty, S., Jones, B. F., & Uzzi, B. (2007). The increasing dominance of teams in production of knowledge. Science, 316(5827), 1036–1039. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1136099

3. Data and methods

3.1 Source and journals

Bibliographic data come from OpenAlex (openalex.org), which describes itself as "a free and open catalog of the world's research" and offers a public API; we collected the data on 17 October 2026. We identified the four journals through OpenAlex's source records by ISSN: Administrative Science Quarterly (0001-8392), Academy of Management Journal (0001-4273), Strategic Management Journal (0143-2095), and Organization Science (1047-7039; online 1526-5455). An earlier version of our notes listed 0170-8406 for Organization Science; in OpenAlex that ISSN belongs to Organization Studies, a different journal. We collected all works whose locations include one of the four journals, published 2008 to 2017, {{v:records_in}} records in all.

3.2 Sample

OpenAlex's document type "article" also includes front matter, book reviews, editorials, comments, and correction notices, and some records are duplicates or attributed to the wrong journal. We applied rules in a fixed order, each record taking the first that applied, and logged every dropped record and changed value with its reason. We dropped {{v:drop_R0}} records whose type is not article or review; {{v:drop_R1}} with no authors in OpenAlex or Crossref, all front matter or unsigned notices; {{v:drop_soshiki}} records from Soshiki Kagaku, a Japanese journal whose English title, Organizational Science, led to their attribution to Organization Science; {{v:drop_copies}} non-publisher copies of records already collected and {{v:drop_unverifiable}} records with no publisher DOI and no journal version in OpenAlex; {{v:drop_R3}} duplicate records and attached correction notices; {{v:drop_R4}} non-research items, including {{v:drop_book_reviews}} book reviews and {{v:drop_amj_editorials}} Academy of Management Journal editorials; {{v:drop_R5}} retracted articles; and {{v:drop_R6}} articles whose corrected publication year falls after 2017. Where OpenAlex had split one paper's citations across duplicate records, we merged them by citing-work identifier so that no citation is counted twice ({{v:merged_dups}} papers). The result is {{v:articles}} research articles: {{v:n_ASQ}} in Administrative Science Quarterly, {{v:n_AMJ}} in Academy of Management Journal, {{v:n_SMJ}} in Strategic Management Journal, and {{v:n_OrgSci}} in Organization Science.

The publication year Y is the year a paper first appeared, usually online ahead of print. In a random check of {{v:date_check_n}} papers against Crossref, OpenAlex's publication year equaled the year the DOI was registered in {{v:date_check_year}}, and the exact date matched in {{v:date_check_day}}. Where OpenAlex's date was suspect (a record merged with a working-paper copy, a volume number inconsistent with the year, or a 1 January placeholder), we used the earliest Crossref date of registration, online, or print publication, which changed the publication year of {{v:year_changes}} papers. Because both Academy of Management Journal and Strategic Management Journal moved to online-first publication during the period, some publication years contain more papers than others; journal-by-year fixed effects absorb these differences.

3.3 Citations

The outcome is the number of citations an article received in the five calendar years after its publication year, Y+1 to Y+5. The publication year itself is excluded because exposure within it ranges from days to almost a full year. Every article's window ends by 2022, so all windows are complete. OpenAlex records a per-year citation field (counts_by_year), but its documentation describes it as covering only the last ten years, and in our data it contains no year before 2012 for any article, so it omits the first years after publication for articles from 2008 to 2011. We therefore counted, for each article, the works that cite it by the citing work's publication year. Citation counts are highly skewed (mean {{v:mean_cites}}, median {{v:median_cites}}; Table 1).

3.4 Authors and countries

Team size is the number of authors. Countries come from authors' affiliations. OpenAlex reports them as ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes, two letters (for example US, GB), according to its documentation for institutions and authorships. Where OpenAlex had no country for an author, we took it from the raw affiliation text only when that text names a country or a US state ({{v:aff_recovered}} authors); institution names alone were not interpreted. A paper is multi-country if its authors' affiliations span two or more countries. This includes a single author affiliated in two countries; a variant that counts only differences between authors is reported in Table 4. Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macao are kept as OpenAlex codes them, separately from mainland China; Section 4.5 shows what recoding them does.

For {{v:n_incomplete}} of the {{v:articles}} articles, at least one author's country remains unknown, so whether the paper is multi-country cannot always be determined. To estimate H1 and H2 on the same papers, we use the complete-case sample of {{v:n_cc}} articles throughout.

3.5 Models

Citations are counts with strong overdispersion (negative binomial dispersion alpha = {{v:alpha}} in the H1 model), so we estimate negative binomial (NB2) models with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. All models include journal-by-year fixed effects, 40 cells, because citation levels and the timing of online-first publication differ by journal and year.

For H1, the main regressor is the natural logarithm of the number of authors, and we report the rate ratio for doubling team size. The logarithm allows each additional author to add less than the last. Among the team-size forms we compared (logarithm, linear count, categories, solo versus team), {{v:ff_best_bic}} fits best by BIC and {{v:ff_best_aic}} by AIC; we report all four.

For H2, the regressor is the multi-country indicator, and team size is controlled with categories (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or more authors), so that "beyond team size" does not rest on a functional form for team size. A version with the logarithm of team size as the control is also reported.

To ask whether either measure is standing in for something else, we add candidate confounders one at a time and together: paper length (log pages), the number of references (log of one plus the count), whether any author is based in the United States, whether the authors span more than one institution, and the largest number of earlier papers any author had published in the sample. Some of these may be consequences of team size rather than causes, so they are checks, not part of the main model. Software: Python {{v:ver_python}} with statsmodels {{v:ver_statsmodels}}, pandas {{v:ver_pandas}}, NumPy {{v:ver_numpy}}, SciPy {{v:ver_scipy}}, patsy {{v:ver_patsy}}, and matplotlib {{v:ver_matplotlib}}.

4. Results

4.1 Descriptive patterns

Table 1 describes the complete-case sample by team size. Mean citations in the five-year window rise from solo papers to four-author papers and are lower for papers with five or more authors. The share of multi-country papers rises steeply up to four authors and is similar for five or more.

Table 1. Complete-case sample by team size

{{TABLE:descriptives}}

4.2 Team size (H1)

Table 2 reports the main models. In column 1, doubling the number of authors is associated with a citation rate {{v:h1_pct}} higher (rate ratio {{v:h1_rr}}, 95% CI {{v:h1_ci}}, p {{v:h1_p}}). Column 2 shows the shape of the association: relative to solo papers, the rate ratio is {{v:cat_2}} for two authors, {{v:cat_3}} for three, {{v:cat_4}} for four, and {{v:cat_5+}} for five or more, and every interval excludes one (Figure 1, panel A). The gain from adding authors rises up to four authors and does not continue beyond it; the five-or-more group is small and its interval is wide. H1 is supported.

Table 2. Main models: citations in years Y+1 to Y+5. Rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals

{{TABLE:main}}

Negative binomial (NB2) models with journal-by-year fixed effects and HC1 standard errors. Team-size categories are relative to solo papers.

[Figure, not shown here: results/stage4/figure1.png] Figure 1

Figure 1. Panel A: rate ratios for teams of two to five or more authors relative to solo papers, with 95% intervals (Table 2, column 2). Panel B: the H1 (circles) and H2 (squares) estimates with 95% intervals under each check in Table 4, on a log scale.

4.3 International reach (H2)

Holding team size fixed with categories, papers whose authors span more than one country have a citation rate {{v:h2_pct}} higher than single-country papers (Table 2, column 3; rate ratio {{v:h2_rr}}, 95% CI {{v:h2_ci}}, p = {{v:h2_p}}). With the logarithm of team size as the control, the estimate is {{v:h2ln_rr}} (p = {{v:h2ln_p}}; column 4). The estimate is positive but its confidence interval includes one. H2 is borderline: the data are consistent with a modest advantage for international teams, but they do not establish one at conventional levels of significance in our main specification.

4.4 Is either measure a proxy for something else?

Table 3 adds candidate confounders. The H1 estimate stays between {{v:proxy_h1_min}} and {{v:proxy_h1_max}} and remains significant in every row (largest p {{v:proxy_h1_pmax}}). The H2 estimate changes little; it ranges from {{v:proxy_h2_min}} to {{v:proxy_h2_max}} and is {{v:proxy_all_h2}} (p = {{v:proxy_all_h2_p}}) with all controls together. Neither measure appears to be standing in for these characteristics. The prior-publication measure counts only papers within our sample, from 2008 onward, and the multiple-institution measure is a lower bound, because authors without a matched institution are not counted.

Table 3. Proxy checks: rate ratios after adding candidate confounders to the main H1 and H2 models

{{TABLE:proxy}}

Each row adds the listed controls to the models in Table 2, columns 1 and 3.

4.5 Robustness

Table 4 and Figure 1, panel B, report the checks. For H1, the rate ratio for doubling team size stays between {{v:rob_h1_min}} and {{v:rob_h1_max}} (largest p {{v:rob_h1_pmax}}) across the full-sample checks; among teams only, it is {{v:teams_h1}} {{v:teams_h1_ci}}. Entered linearly, each additional author is associated with a {{v:lin_pct}} higher citation rate, and team papers have a rate ratio of {{v:team_h1}} {{v:team_h1_ci}} relative to solo papers.

For H2, the estimate stays between {{v:rob_h2_min}} and {{v:rob_h2_max}} in every full-sample check, with p-values between {{v:rob_h2_pmin}} and {{v:rob_h2_pmax}}. It is significant at the 5% level with clustered standard errors ({{v:clus_h2}}, p = {{v:clus_h2_p}}) and with capped citations ({{v:wins_h2}}, p = {{v:wins_h2_p}}), and not in the other checks. The size of the H2 estimate is stable; its significance is not.

Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macao are coded separately from mainland China in OpenAlex, so a paper with authors in, say, Hong Kong and Taiwan counts as multi-country. Of the complete-case articles, {{v:tw_n}} have an author based in Taiwan: {{v:tw_multi}} of them are multi-country, {{v:tw_only}} have all authors in Taiwan, and {{v:tw_cn_only}} pair Taiwan only with mainland China; {{v:hkmo_n}} articles have an author in Hong Kong or Macao. Recoding all three as China changes the multi-country status of {{v:flip_n}} articles, {{v:flip_tw}} of them involving Taiwan, and moves the H2 estimate to {{v:cn_h2}} {{v:cn_h2_ci}}. Their coding does not affect the results.

Table 4. Robustness checks

{{TABLE:robustness}}

H1: rate ratio for doubling team size, except where the row names another estimand (per additional author; team versus solo). H2: rate ratio for multi-country papers, controlling team-size categories. The last three rows use a random subsample of {{v:sub_all_n}} articles and its complement ({{v:comp_n}} articles); see Section 4.6.

4.6 Self-citations: a partial check

Larger teams have more authors who can cite the paper, so part of the team-size association could be mechanical. We counted citations excluding self-citations, defined as citing works that list any of the article's authors by OpenAlex identifier. Our data allowance permitted this for a seeded random subsample of {{v:sub_all_n}} complete-case articles only; the remaining {{v:comp_n}} could not be fetched, and nothing was substituted for them. This check is therefore partial.

In the subsample, the mean share of window citations that are self-citations rises with team size: {{v:self_1}} for solo papers, {{v:self_2}} for two authors, {{v:self_3}} for three, {{v:self_4}} for four, and {{v:self_5}} for five or more. For H1, removing self-citations moves the rate ratio for doubling team size from {{v:sub_all_h1}} {{v:sub_all_h1_ci}} to {{v:sub_ns_h1}} {{v:sub_ns_h1_ci}}: self-citation accounts for a small part of the team-size association, not most of it.

H2 cannot be assessed in the subsample. With all citations, before self-citations are removed, the subsample's H2 estimate is already {{v:sub_all_h2}} {{v:sub_all_h2_ci}}, against {{v:comp_h2}} {{v:comp_h2_ci}} in the other {{v:comp_n}} articles. The difference between the two halves is within what chance produces (difference in log rate ratios {{v:split_h2_d}}, SE {{v:split_h2_se}}, p = {{v:split_h2_p}}, treating the halves as independent), so the subsample appears noisy rather than different. But it cannot tell us whether self-citations matter for H2.

4.7 Differences across journals

Table 5 estimates the models separately by journal. The team-size association is significant in Strategic Management Journal and Organization Science and not in Administrative Science Quarterly or Academy of Management Journal. The multi-country estimate is positive in all four journals and significant in none. A pooled test does not reject equal slopes across journals for either hypothesis (H1 p = {{v:wald_h1_p}}; H2 p = {{v:wald_h2_p}}), so the pooled estimates are a reasonable summary, though the journal-level samples are small, especially for Administrative Science Quarterly.

Table 5. Journal-specific estimates

{{TABLE:journals}}

Separate negative binomial models for each journal with year fixed effects and HC1 standard errors. The equal-slopes test is a Wald test of the journal interactions in the pooled model with journal-by-year fixed effects.

5. Discussion

In four leading management journals, papers by more authors are cited more in the five years after publication, with the gain concentrated in the move from solo to small teams. The association holds across our proxy and robustness checks, and only a small part of it is attributable to self-citation in the subsample where we could measure it. This is consistent with the patterns reported by Wuchty et al. (2007) and Larivière et al. (2015), although our design differs from theirs and the estimates are not directly comparable.

The evidence on international reach is weaker. Papers spanning more than one country have a citation rate about {{v:h2_pct}} higher than single-country papers of the same team size, an estimate that is stable in size across every specification we tried, but whose confidence interval includes one in the main model and in most checks. We read this as borderline: the data do not rule out a modest advantage for international teams, and they do not establish one. One possible reason is that international collaboration is so closely tied to team size here that, once size is held fixed, little independent variation remains to estimate it precisely.

Limitations

Self-citations: partial check. Self-citations could be removed only for a random subsample of {{v:sub_all_n}} of the {{v:n_cc}} articles. The check informs H1 but not H2, and should be completed on the full sample.

Income-group extension dropped. We planned to ask whether it matters that a team includes an author based in a country outside the World Bank's high-income group. This requires each country's income group in each publication year from 2008 to 2017. The World Bank's data API, which we could reach, returned only the current classification in our tests: a request for Chile in 2010 returned Chile's current group, and so did the April 2010 edition in its archive of World Development Indicators. A historical classification would be needed [Unverified: we understand the World Bank publishes one as the file OGHIST.xlsx, "Historical classification by income," with its Country and Lending Groups data; the host serving it could not be reached, so we could not confirm the file or its contents]. We did not use the current classification as a substitute, because the groups in force in 2008 to 2017 may differ from it and we could not check by how much. The extension is therefore left out of this paper.

Observational design. The associations we estimate are not causal effects. Teams may form around more promising projects, and international teams may differ in topic or method in ways our controls do not capture.

Data coverage and measurement. All bibliographic data and citation counts come from OpenAlex as of 17 October 2026, and are only as complete as its records. Duplicate copies of a paper were matched by title and authors, so a copy under a different title can escape matching; we found one such case while checking the paper, a working-paper copy of a Strategic Management Journal article, and merged it by hand, and others may remain. Countries come from affiliations, which may not reflect where authors live or work. {{v:n_incomplete}} articles with an author of unknown country are excluded from the analysis. Publication years were corrected only for records we had already collected, so a paper that OpenAlex dates to 2007 but that appeared in 2008 is not in the sample.

Scope. The sample covers four leading journals, and the results may not hold for management research published elsewhere.

Multiple checks. We report many robustness checks without correcting for multiple comparisons. They are meant to show how stable the estimates are rather than to provide separate tests, which is why we describe H2 as borderline rather than supported.

References

Larivière, V., Gingras, Y., Sugimoto, C. R., & Tsou, A. (2015). Team size matters: Collaboration and scientific impact since 1900. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 66(7), 1323–1332. https://doi.org/10.1002/asi.23266

Wuchty, S., Jones, B. F., & Uzzi, B. (2007). The increasing dominance of teams in production of knowledge. Science, 316(5827), 1036–1039. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1136099

Data sources

Crossref REST API, api.crossref.org, accessed 17 October 2026.

OpenAlex, openalex.org, API accessed 17 October 2026.

"""Stage 5: build paper.md from paper_src.md and the result files.

paper_src.md is the hand-written text. It contains two kinds of placeholder: {{TABLE:name}} replaced by a markdown table generated here from a results CSV {{v:name}} replaced by a single number taken from a results or data file Every number in the paper that comes from the analysis is a placeholder; the script fails if any placeholder is unknown or left unresolved.

Sources (read only): results/stage4/*.csv analysis results (scripts/analysis.py) data/analysis/summary.json sample and cleaning counts (scripts/build_dataset.py) data/analysis/cleaning_log.csv cleaning counts by reason Outputs: paper.md the paper results/stage5/paper_values.csv every value substituted, with its source

Usage: venv/bin/python -I scripts/make_paper.py """

import csv import json import os import re

import pandas as pd

R4 = "results/stage4" VALUES, SOURCES = {}, {}

def put(name, value, source): VALUES[name] = value SOURCES[name] = source

def rr(x): return f"{x:.3f}"

def ci(lo, hi): return f"[{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]"

def pval(p): return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

def pct(x): return f"{x * 100:.1f}%"

def md(header, rows): out = ["| " + " | ".join(header) + " |", "|" + "|".join("---" for _ in header) + "|"] out += ["| " + " | ".join(str(c) for c in r) + " |" for r in rows] return "\n".join(out)

------------------------------------------------------------------ values

put("rob_h2_pmax", f"{t4.loc[h2vars, 'h2_p'].max():.3f}", "table4 max H2 p")
for key, v in (("teams", "teams only (2+ authors)"), ("pois", "Poisson PML"),

               ("comp", "complement of subsample: all citations")):
    r = t4.loc[v]
    put(f"{key}_h1", rr(r.h1_irr), f"table4 {v}"); put(f"{key}_h1_ci", ci(r.h1_lo, r.h1_hi), f"table4 {v}")
    put(f"{key}_h2", rr(r.h2_irr), f"table4 {v}"); put(f"{key}_h2_ci", ci(r.h2_lo, r.h2_hi), f"table4 {v}")
    put(f"{key}_h2_p", pval(r.h2_p), f"table4 {v}"); put(f"{key}_n", f"{int(r.n):,}", f"table4 {v}")
lin = t4.loc["linear author count (per author, H1)"]
put("lin_h1", rr(lin.h1_irr), "table4 linear"); put("lin_pct", f"{(lin.h1_irr - 1) * 100:.1f}%", "table4 linear")
team = t4.loc["solo vs team (H1: team vs solo)"]
put("team_h1", rr(team.h1_irr), "table4 solo vs team"); put("team_h1_ci", ci(team.h1_lo, team.h1_hi), "table4")

t4c = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table4c_subsample_vs_complement.csv").set_index("hypothesis")
put("split_h2_d", f"{t4c.loc['H2', 'log_rr_complement_minus_subsample']:.3f}", "table4c H2")
put("split_h2_se", f"{t4c.loc['H2', 'se']:.3f}", "table4c H2"); put("split_h2_p", f"{t4c.loc['H2', 'p']:.2f}", "table4c H2")
t4b = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table4b_self_citations.csv", index_col=0)
put("self_solo", pct(t4b.loc["1", "mean_self_share"]), "table4b 1.mean_self_share")
put("self_5", pct(t4b.loc["5+", "mean_self_share"]), "table4b 5+.mean_self_share")
for k in ("1", "2", "3", "4"):
    put(f"self_{k}", pct(t4b.loc[k, "mean_self_share"]), f"table4b {k}.mean_self_share")

w = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table5b_wald_equal_slopes.csv").set_index("hypothesis")
put("wald_h1_p", f"{w.loc['H1', 'p']:.3f}", "table5b H1"); put("wald_h2_p", f"{w.loc['H2', 'p']:.3f}", "table5b H2")
put("wald_h1_chi2", f"{w.loc['H1', 'chi2']:.2f}", "table5b H1"); put("wald_h2_chi2", f"{w.loc['H2', 'chi2']:.2f}", "table5b H2")

sw = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/software_versions.csv").set_index("package")["version"]
for p in sw.index:
    put(f"ver_{p}", sw[p], "software_versions.csv (written by analysis.py at run time)")

t6 = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table6_taiwan_hk_mo.csv").set_index("quantity")["value"]
put("tw_n", t6["complete-case articles with a Taiwan (TW) author"], "table6")
put("tw_multi", t6["  of which multi-country as coded (TW distinct)"], "table6")
put("tw_only", t6["  of which all authors in TW"], "table6")
put("tw_cn_only", t6["  of which TW is the only other country besides CN"], "table6")
put("hkmo_n", t6["articles with an HK or MO author"], "table6")
put("flip_n", t6["articles whose multi-country status changes if TW, HK, MO coded as CN"], "table6")
put("flip_tw", t6["  of which involve TW"], "table6")

------------------------------------------------------------------ tables

def tables(): T = {} t1 = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table1_descriptives.csv", index_col=0) T["descriptives"] = md( ["Authors", "Articles", "Mean citations, Y+1 to Y+5", "Median", "Share multi-country", "Mean countries"], [[("All" if i == "all" else i), f"{int(r.articles):,}", f"{r.mean_cites_5yr:.1f}", f"{r.median_cites_5yr:.0f}", pct(r.share_multi_country), f"{r.mean_countries:.2f}"] for i, r in t1.iterrows()])

t2 = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table2_main.csv")
cols = ["H1 (ln authors)", "H1 (size categories)", "H2 (size categories)", "H2 (ln authors)"]
terms = ["doubling team size", "2 authors vs 1", "3 authors vs 1", "4 authors vs 1", "5+ authors vs 1",
         "multi-country"]
rows = []
for t in terms:
    cells = []
    for c in cols:
        r = t2[(t2["model"] == c) & (t2["term"] == t)]
        cells.append(f"{rr(r.irr.iloc[0])} {ci(r.lo.iloc[0], r.hi.iloc[0])}" if len(r) else "")
    rows.append([t] + cells)
meta = {c: t2[t2["model"] == c].iloc[0] for c in cols}
rows.append(["Dispersion (alpha)"] + [f"{meta[c].alpha:.3f}" for c in cols])
rows.append(["AIC"] + [f"{meta[c].aic:,.1f}" for c in cols])
rows.append(["N"] + [f"{int(meta[c].n):,}" for c in cols])
T["main"] = md(["", "(1) H1: ln authors", "(2) H1: size categories", "(3) H2: size categories",
                "(4) H2: ln authors"], rows)

t3 = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table3_proxy_checks.csv")
T["proxy"] = md(["Controls added", "H1: doubling team size", "p", "H2: multi-country", "p"],
                [[r.controls, r["H1 doubling team size"], pval(r["H1 p"]), r["H2 multi-country"], pval(r["H2 p"])]
                 for _, r in t3.iterrows()])

t4 = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table4_robustness.csv")
# The H1 estimand is named in the row label where it is not "doubling" (see the table note).
T["robustness"] = md(["Check", "H1 rate ratio [95% CI]", "p", "H2 rate ratio [95% CI]", "p", "N"],
                     [[r.variant, f"{rr(r.h1_irr)} {ci(r.h1_lo, r.h1_hi)}", pval(r.h1_p),
                       f"{rr(r.h2_irr)} {ci(r.h2_lo, r.h2_hi)}", pval(r.h2_p), f"{int(r.n):,}"]
                      for _, r in t4.iterrows()])

t5 = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table5_journal_specific.csv")
names = {"ASQ": "Administrative Science Quarterly", "AMJ": "Academy of Management Journal",
         "SMJ": "Strategic Management Journal", "OrgSci": "Organization Science"}
w = pd.read_csv(f"{R4}/table5b_wald_equal_slopes.csv").set_index("hypothesis")
rows = [[names[r.journal], f"{int(r.n):,}", r["H1 doubling team size"], pval(r["H1 p"]), r["H2 multi-country"],
         pval(r["H2 p"])] for _, r in t5.iterrows()]
rows.append(["Test of equal slopes (pooled, 3 df)", "", f"chi2 = {w.loc['H1', 'chi2']:.2f}",
             f"{w.loc['H1', 'p']:.3f}", f"chi2 = {w.loc['H2', 'chi2']:.2f}", f"{w.loc['H2', 'p']:.3f}"])
T["journals"] = md(["Journal", "N", "H1: doubling team size", "p", "H2: multi-country", "p"], rows)

return T

def main(): load_values() T = tables() src = open("paper_src.md").read() missing = []

def sub(m):
    kind, name = m.group(1), m.group(2)
    pool = T if kind == "TABLE" else VALUES
    if name not in pool:
        missing.append(m.group(0))
        return m.group(0)
    return str(pool[name])

out = re.sub(r"\{\{(TABLE|v):([A-Za-z0-9_+]+)\}\}", sub, src)
left = re.findall(r"\{\{[^}]*\}\}", out)
if missing or left:
    raise SystemExit(f"unresolved placeholders: {sorted(set(missing + left))}")
header = ("<!-- Generated by scripts/make_paper.py from paper_src.md and results/stage4. "
          "Do not edit by hand; edit paper_src.md and re-run. -->\n\n")
with open("paper.md", "w") as f:
    f.write(header + out)
os.makedirs("results/stage5", exist_ok=True)
with open("results/stage5/paper_values.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    wr = csv.writer(f)
    wr.writerow(["name", "value", "source"])
    for k in sorted(VALUES):
        wr.writerow([k, VALUES[k], SOURCES[k]])
used = set(re.findall(r"\{\{v:([A-Za-z0-9_+]+)\}\}", src))
print(f"paper.md written: {len(out.split())} words; {len(used)} values and "
      f"{len(set(re.findall(r'{{TABLE:([a-z]+)}}', src)))} tables substituted")

if name == "main": main()
